issues.legal_issue: A financial corporation enforcing security over charged assets must conduct a reasonable sale that seeks the best possible price and realizes sale proceeds for distribution among those entitled to them.
material_facts: The corporation held the first charge over the flour mill’s assets, while another creditor held a second charge.

The corporation agreed to transfer the assets without obtaining or producing a valuation, and the proposed consideration was pegged to the corporation’s debt and included a promise to pay the second creditor rather than realized proceeds.
The assets were handed to the proposed buyer before the tender deadline and before the bids were opened.
The corporation did not call for matching offers from the company’s directors, promoters or guarantors.
The corporation did not realize and distribute the full sale consideration.
issues.conclusion: The agreement and transfer breached the corporation’s statutory duties and were invalid; the corporation had failed to act fairly or reasonably to secure the best possible price and protect the interests of the subsequent charge-holder and the mortgagor.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 29(1) and (4) of the State Financial Corporations Act, 1951, a corporation enforcing its security must sell the charged property and apply realized proceeds first to its properly incurred costs and its debt, with the residue paid to those entitled to it. A charge creates a right to payment from the property or its proceeds, not an interest in the property itself (Transfer of Property Act, section 100). The corporation must seek the best possible price, understood as fair market value; adequate publicity and maximum participation in a public sale help achieve it. The Court relied on M/s S.J.S. Business Enterprises (P) Ltd. v. State of Bihar, which affirmed the approach in Chairman and Managing Director, SIPCOT v. Contromix Pvt. Ltd. and Haryana Financial State Corporation v. Jagdamba Oil Mills; it also relied on Pannalal Binjraj v. Union of India on abuse of statutory power, Rajah Kishendatt Ram v. Rajah Mumtaz Ali Khan on the treatment of surplus proceeds, and M.C. Chacko v. State Bank of Travancore and Subbu Chetti v. Arunachalam Chettiar on promises to discharge a third party’s debt.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_enforcement_sale and secured_assets_have_multiple_chargeholders and sale_not_independently_valued and (assets_transferred_before_bidding_closed or consideration_includes_unrealized_third_party_promise) and sale_proceeds_not_realized_for_distribution

predicates.appeal_challenges_enforcement_sale: An appeal challenges a financial corporation’s sale of assets while enforcing security for a debt.
predicates.secured_assets_have_multiple_chargeholde: The assets securing the debt are also subject to claims held by other creditors or the owner.
predicates.sale_not_independently_valued: The corporation did not establish the assets’ value through an independent valuation before agreeing to sell them.
predicates.assets_transferred_before_bidding_closed: The corporation transferred possession of the assets before the announced bidding process had concluded.
predicates.consideration_includes_unrealized_third_: The agreed consideration includes a buyer’s promise to pay a separate creditor instead of payment realized by the corporation.
predicates.sale_proceeds_not_realized_for_distribut: The corporation did not realize sale proceeds and distribute them among those entitled to payment.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an enforcement sale of multiply encumbered assets and the corporation fails to value them, transfers them before bidding closes or accepts an unrealized promise, and does not realize proceeds for distribution, the sale is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A mortgagor’s right to redeem is not extinguished merely because property is put up for auction or an agreement for sale is made; absent a completed conveyance, payment of the secured debt preserves the right to redeem.
material_facts: The company’s assets were subject to a mortgage and the company retained an equity of redemption.
The corporation had put the assets up for tender and entered into an agreement for sale, but no conveyance had been executed.
The appellant, acting as a director of the company, paid the corporation’s full dues before the tenders were opened and sought the return of the company’s title documents and assets.
The corporation did not return the assets and instead adjusted the payment to the account of another company.
issues.conclusion: The company retained its right to redeem because no conveyance had extinguished that right; payment of the corporation’s dues required the loan to be treated as repaid, and the assets were to be restored to the company.
issues.legal_principle: Under the principles governing a mortgagor’s equity of redemption, an agreement for sale does not by itself extinguish that equity; extinguishment requires a completed conveyance. Putting property up for auction likewise does not extinguish the right of redemption. The Court relied on section 69 of the Transfer of Property Act, Mulla on Transfer of Property, and Narandas Karsondas v. S.A. Kamtam.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_enforcement_sale and mortgaged_assets_have_not_been_conveyed and secured_debt_is_paid and mortgagor_seeks_redemption

predicates.appeal_challenges_enforcement_sale: An appeal challenges a financial corporation’s sale of assets while enforcing security for a debt.
predicates.mortgaged_assets_have_not_been_conveyed: The mortgaged assets have not been transferred by a completed conveyance.
predicates.secured_debt_is_paid: The secured debt is paid on behalf of the mortgagor.
predicates.mortgagor_seeks_redemption: The mortgagor seeks return of the mortgaged assets after paying the secured debt.

issues.definition: When an enforcement sale is challenged, the assets have not been conveyed, the secured debt is paid, and the mortgagor seeks their return, the mortgagor retains the right to redeem.

issues.legal_issue: A financial corporation’s unexplained delivery of charged assets to a proposed buyer before a public tender closes, in circumstances indicating a prearranged sale, can constitute collusion and misuse of its authority.
material_facts: The corporation invited tenders with a stated closing and bid-opening schedule but handed possession of the assets to the proposed buyer before those stages occurred.
The buyer’s payment included demand drafts dated before its offer to purchase, and the corporation did not explain how the buyer could have obtained those drafts before making its offer.

The corporation asserted that the assets had been handed over subject to their return if a higher tender offer emerged, but that condition appeared neither in the tender committee’s minutes nor in the later sale agreement.
The corporation did not produce a board resolution authorizing the early transfer and did not call for matching offers.
The corporation returned the appellant’s earnest money after the appellant went to court, although the record showed that the appellant had refused to collect it.
issues.conclusion: The circumstances indicated collusion between the corporation and the proposed buyer, and the corporation had misused its authority by acting on extraneous matters and ignoring relevant ones; its acts were ultra vires.
issues.legal_principle: Statutory powers vested in a public financial corporation must be exercised bona fide, fairly and reasonably. Circumstances that reasonably suggest abuse of power may rebut the presumption that public officials acted honestly, and an absence of a credible explanation may support a finding that the action was improper. The Court relied on M/s S.J.S. Business Enterprises (P) Ltd. v. State of Bihar and Pannalal Binjraj v. Union of India; it also relied on Express Newspapers Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India for the principle that action based on extraneous matters and disregard of relevant matters may be ultra vires.

rule.if: appeal_challenges_public_authority_sale and assets_delivered_before_tender_closed and buyer_payment_predates_buyer_offer and early_transfer_lacks_documented_condition and authority_lacks_credible_explanation

predicates.appeal_challenges_public_authority_sale: An appeal challenges a public authority’s sale of secured assets.
predicates.assets_delivered_before_tender_closed: The authority delivered possession of the assets before the announced tender process had concluded.
predicates.buyer_payment_predates_buyer_offer: The buyer’s payment instruments were dated before the buyer made its offer to purchase.
predicates.early_transfer_lacks_documented_conditio: The authority’s asserted condition governing an early transfer was not recorded in the relevant sale documents or committee records.
predicates.authority_lacks_credible_explanation: The authority did not credibly explain the circumstances surrounding the early transfer and sale.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a public authority’s sale and the authority delivers assets before tender closes, the buyer’s payment predates its offer, the asserted transfer condition is undocumented, and the authority lacks a credible explanation, the authority’s action is collusive and ultra vires.
